historical_record.description: The Gold Rush–era ship Tonquin sank in San Francisco Bay in 1849; an 1853 U.S. Coast Survey chart places the wreck at roughly this site.
The Gold Rush–era ship Carlota, sunk in 1850, may also lie within or near the site; a third wreck, the Samoset (sunk 1852), was once placed in the area but judged unlikely to be here.

The site was originally part of the bay's shallow margin; the area was filled gradually from the 1850s, and the timber retaining wall the wharf sits on was built between 1880 and 1893. The site was not occupied until the wharf went up in 1919.

The State Board of Harbor Commissioners built Wharf J-10 for the fishing industry: a Mission Revival wood-frame fish-processing building with eight arched recessed openings and a red-tile skirt roof, designed by A.A. Pyle and erected in two phases on wood piles over a wood substructure with a concrete topping slab, housing fish-packing departments, storerooms, waterside docking and offices.

The building stayed in continuous use for net storage and fish packing. The F. Alioto Fish Company was a long-term tenant traceable to at least the 1940s; other tenants included the fish wholesalers Standard Fisheries Corporation, Consolidated Fisheries and the California Shell Fish Company (Cal Shell), and Oswald Machine Works, a diesel-engine distributor.
The east end of the building was repaired after fire damage; over its life the building also gained interior mezzanines and replacement doors and windows.

After an engineering study found the wharf's structural elements in danger of imminent collapse, the Port issued a notice to vacate and condemned the building; the remaining tenants, the F. Alioto Fish Company and Cal Shell, had to leave, utilities were cut, and steel bracing was installed to shore the northwest corner.

A historic-resources evaluation for the Port identified Wharf J-10 together with 2907–2909 and 2911 Jones Street as potentially eligible for the California Register as a small historic district, significant for the boat-building and fishing industries along Fisherman's Wharf from the 1910s through the early 1940s; the wharf was also listed as a contributor in the Planning Department's draft Fisherman's Wharf Area Plan, which was never adopted.
Between 500 and 1,000 square feet of the wharf decking at the northwest corner collapsed into the water.
A fire charred three truss structures at the east end of the vacant building, one substantially; firefighters removed roughly 5 to 10 percent of the roof for access.

unknowns: The assessor's roll dates the structure on this parcel to 1900; the wharf was built in 1919.
